content: Folic acid, along with vitamins A, D, E, and B6, as well as calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, and dietary fiber, are essential components of a healthy diet. However, excessive consumption of fat, sodium, cholesterol, and added sugars should be avoided. Barriers to maintaining a healthy diet may include physical, economic, and socio-cultural factors, as well as a lack of knowledge and self-efficacy. Eating disorders, such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia, often emerge during adolescence, particularly among girls, and are more prevalent in high-income countries. These disorders are characterized by abnormal eating behaviors, an intense preoccupation with food, and an obsession with weight and body shape. They can result in severe physical and mental health consequences, including high rates of comorbidities such as depression, anxiety, and substance abuse. Multidimensional programs that combine traditional health education with broader mental health promotion strategies have shown promising outcomes. Adolescents are increasingly exposed to unhealthy food environments and aggressive marketing of unhealthy foods through television, films, social media, and point-of-sale advertising. This has led to higher consumption of inexpensive, energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods that are high in sugar, sodium, and fat, including processed and ultra-processed foods. Many adolescents lack access to affordable fresh fruits and vegetables and may not have the nutritional knowledge, skills, or resources to purchase and prepare healthy foods. Efforts should focus on promoting the consumption of fruits and vegetables while discouraging the intake of energy-dense, micronutrient-poor foods and sugar-sweetened beverages. Reducing adolescents' exposure to heavy marketing of unhealthy products and providing them with the necessary information and skills to make healthy food choices are additional measures to improve adolescent nutrition. Examples of micronutrient-rich foods include: Iron: Heme iron from meat, poultry, and fish is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron from cereals, pulses, legumes, fruits, and vegetables. Consuming non-heme iron with vitamin C-rich foods enhances absorption, while calcium inhibits iron absorption and should not be consumed simultaneously. Calcium: Found in leafy green vegetables, fish eaten whole, soy products, and dairy. Oxalic acid in spinach, beetroot, and sweet potatoes limits calcium bioavailability. Diets high in animal protein, phytates (found in whole grains and legumes), or sodium can reduce calcium absorption. Potassium: Found in leafy greens, root vegetables, beans, peas, vine-based fruits (e.g., tomatoes, cucumbers), and tree fruits. Zinc: Found in nuts, legumes, whole grains, seeds, shellfish, poultry, eggs, red meat, and dairy. Phytates in plant-based diets and supplements of iron or calcium can inhibit zinc absorption. Vitamin A: Found in deeply colored fruits and vegetables, oily fruits, and red palm oil. Intestinal infections, diarrhea, and alcohol consumption can limit absorption. Vitamin C: Found in citrus fruits, bell peppers, green beans, strawberries, papaya, guava, kiwi, potatoes, broccoli, and tomatoes. Vitamin D: Found in oily fish, liver, egg yolks, yeast, and mushrooms. Sunlight is the most potent source of vitamin D. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends reducing free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% for additional health benefits. Potassium intake should be increased to control blood pressure, while sodium intake should be reduced to less than 2 grams per day in adults, with adjustments for children based on energy requirements. Micronutrient deficiencies, such as iron, folic acid, vitamin A, and vitamin B12, are common among adolescents. Iron deficiency anemia, which affects nearly 40% of girls aged 15–19 in some countries, reduces physical capacity and work performance and is a leading cause of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost globally. Entering pregnancy with suboptimal iron reserves increases the risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Iodine deficiency, the second-largest micronutrient burden among adolescents, can lead to goiter and impair fetal neurological development during pregnancy. Vitamin A deficiency is among the top 15 causes of global mortality and morbidity. WHO guidelines recommend fortifying staple foods, such as maize flour and salt, with micronutrients like iron, folic acid, and iodine to prevent deficiencies. Daily iron supplementation is advised for menstruating adolescent girls and women in areas with high anemia prevalence. Intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation is also recommended in such settings.
